newsitem.title: USA: Laborers' chief Coia wins union's first election.
newsitem.headline: Laborers' chief Coia wins union's first election.

text.p: Laborers' International Union of North America (LIUNA) President Arthur Coia won a full five-year term Thursday in the 93-year-old union's first election that was open to its members.

Coia, a supporter of President Clinton and Democrats and who has come under the scrutiny of congressional Republicans, received about 67 perecent of the ballots cast, the union said. His opponent, Bruno Caruso who heads a LIUNA local in Chicago, got 33 percent, it said.

"This is a victory for the hard-working men and women of this great union," said Coia. "It is also a clear vote of confidence for the internal reform efforts we began two years ago in cooperation with the U.S. Department of Justice."
The election, which was conducted by a government approved election officer, was required as part of a package of reforms agreed upon by union and the Justice Department in February.

Fewer than 10 percent of the union's 750,000 members voted during balloting period between Nov. 2 and Dec. 16, LIUNA said. But 78 percent of those voting favored direct elections for members of the union's General Executive Board in the future, it said.
Previously officers of LIUNA, which is alleged to have been controlled by the Chicago mob for about 70 years, were elected by convention delegates.

Justice Department officials had credited the union with taking substantial steps to rid itself of mob influence and last summer defended their agreement with LIUNA against Republican charges that it was a "sweetheart" deal that allowed Coia to keep his job because of his relationship with Clinton.
Clinton has golfed with Coia, exchanged notes with him and invited him to the White House.

Coia, 53, a lawyer from Rhode Island, was elected LIUNA general president nearly four years ago after spending another four years in its No. 2 job of secretary-treasurer, a post previously held by his father.
Under his leadership, the union has become more aggressive in organizing new members, especially in the South. He chairs the organizing committee of the AFL-CIO Executive Council.
LIUNA represents U.S. and Canadian workers in the construction, manufacturing, health care, service and hazardous waste industries as well as in the government.
